﴿He said: "My Lord, I have called my people night and day.﴾ ﴿But my calling only increased them in flight.﴾ ﴿And whenever I called them that You might forgive them, they put their fingers in their ears, covered themselves with their garments, persisted, and became arrogantly proud.﴾ ﴿Then I called them openly.﴾ ﴿Then I spoke to them publicly and I also confided to them in private.﴾ ﴿So I said: Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed He is Ever-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain.﴾

This statement was made by Nuh (peace be upon him) after his lifespan had been prolonged and despair about his people had been confirmed. His words "night and day" are an expression for the continuity of his calling and that he never tired of it at any time. It is narrated from Qatadah that Nuh (peace be upon him) would be approached by a man from his people with his son, and the man would say to his son: "O my son, beware of this man, for my father warned me against him," and he would tell him that he is a madman.

Shibl narrated from Ibn Kathir a reading with a fatha on the ya' and without a hamza, like "hudaya" (هُدايَ). 'Asim also, along with Ya'qub and Salam, read it with a hamza and a sakin ya' (ياء ساكنة).

His words, glorified is He, ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ may be taken literally, and may also be an expression for their turning away and their strong rejection of his words and his calling. Likewise His words, exalted is He, ﴿and covered themselves with their garments﴾, meaning they made them into coverings over their heads. Al-Israr (الإصْرار, persistence) is steadfastness upon a particular belief, and its usage is mostly for sins.

Then he repeated the description of his calling to them, for clarification and emphasis. "Openly" (جِهارًا) means publicly, in gatherings. "Al-Israr" (الإسْرار, confiding) is what was of his calling in which he addressed individuals between himself and them in private, and this is the utmost seriousness. His words, ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾... ﴿He will send the sky﴾, imply that seeking forgiveness is a cause for rain to descend upon every community. It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that he asked people to pray for rain, and he did no more than seek forgiveness for an hour and then departed. A group of people said to him: "We did not see you ask for rain, O Commander of the Faithful." He said: "By Allah, I sought the descent of rain with the constellations of the sky," and then he recited this verse (may Allah be pleased with him). A man complained to al-Hasan about drought, and he said to him: "Seek forgiveness from Allah." Another complained to him of poverty, and he said: "Seek forgiveness from Allah, glorified is He." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 71, verse 12–20:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿He will increase you in wealth and children, and will appoint for you gardens and will appoint for you rivers.﴾ ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect for Allah any dignity?﴾ ﴿And He has created you in stages.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp.﴾ ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth a growth.﴾ ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth [again] a bringing forth.﴾ ﴿And Allah has made for you the earth a spread-out expanse.﴾ ﴿That you may traverse therein roads, wide ways.﴾

He promised them wealth, children, gardens and rivers because of their love for this world. People differed concerning the meaning of the words of the Exalted, relating from Noah (peace be upon him): ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect for Allah any dignity?﴾ Abu 'Ubayda and others said: its meaning is "you do not fear," and from this is the verse of the Hudhali:

"When the bee stings him, he does not fear its sting, and he opposes it in a house of cloth, working [in it]."

They said: "al-Waqar" is greatness and authority, so the statement, on this view, is a threat and intimidation. Some scholars said: "tarjuna" retains its meaning of hoping, as if he said: "What is the matter with you that you do not make your hope in Allah the Exalted and in meeting Him," and "waqaran" would be, on this interpretation, from them, as if he said: "a composure from you and a steadiness in reflection," because disbelief implies levity, recklessness and headstrong conduct. As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And He has created you in stages﴾, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it is a reference to the gradual development that the human undergoes in the belly of his mother: from the drop, to the clot, to the lump. A group of the interpreters said: it is a reference to the lesson in the differences of people's colours, forms and religions. "Atwar" means the varying states, and from it is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"If he recovers, his blindness has flown away; and a man creates stage after stage."

The majority read "alam tarawu" with the ta', while a group read it with the ya', as the verb of the absent third person. As for "tibaqan," it is said to be a verbal noun, meaning "congruence," that each one is a layer for the other, and similar to the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"... he layered the earth, [the rain] searched and spread out."

It is also said to be the plural of "tabaq," and it is an adjective of "sab'" (seven). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "tibaqin" in the genitive as an adjective of "samawat." As for the words of the Exalted: "wa ja'ala al-qamara fihinna nuran" (and made the moon therein a light), it is permissible because the moon, insofar as it is in one of them, is in all of them. It is related that the moon is in the lowest heaven. 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas and 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with them, said: the sun and the moon have their backs toward the earth, and the approach of their light and its elevation in the sky is what the word "siraj" (lamp) implies. It is said that the sun is in the fifth heaven, and it is said: in the fourth. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: it is in the fourth in winter, and in the seventh in summer.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has caused you to grow from the earth a growth﴾, it is a metaphor, insofar as Adam (peace be upon him) was taken from the earth, and then all of them came to grow from him. The word "nabatan" (a growth) is a verbal noun that comes from a source other than the verb, and the implied sense is: "fa-nabattum nabatan" (so you grew a growth). "The return into it" is by burial in it, which is the custom of mankind, and "the bringing forth" is the resurrection on the Day of Judgement for the place of standing, reckoning and recompense.

As for the words of the Exalted: "bisatan" (a spread-out expanse), its apparent meaning implies that the earth is flat, not spherical. Holding either of the two views does not in itself harm the Sharia, except that a corrupt reasoning be built upon the claim of sphericity. As for the belief that it is flat, it is the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah the Exalted, and it is that from which no corruption whatsoever arises. Ibn Mujahid argued for the soundness of this by the water of the encompassing sea surrounding the inhabited world, saying: "If the earth were spherical, the water would not remain upon it." "Subul" means the paths, and "fijaj" means the wide ones.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Nuh said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him only in loss."﴾ ﴿And they have plotted a great plot.﴾ ﴿And they said, "Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd, or Suwa', or Yaghuth, or Ya'uq, or Nasr."﴾ ﴿And they have already led many astray. The meaning: When they did not obey, and Nuh (peace be upon him) despaired of their faith, Nuh said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed their nobles and misguided leaders." He described them by saying that their wealth and children increased them only in loss, that is, in ruin.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi' (in the narration of Kharija from him) recited "wa-wulduhu" with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. This is the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-Nakha'i, and Mujahid. Nafi', 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir recited "wa-waladuhu" with a fatha on the waw and the lam, and both have the same meaning, like bukhl and bakhal. This is the reading of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Thabit, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba. He also recited "wa-wilduhu" with a kasra on the waw, and this is the reading of al-Jahdari, Zirr, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Talha. Abu 'Amr said: "wuld" with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam means the clan and the people. Abu Hatim said: it is possible that "al-wuld" with a damma on the waw is the plural of "al-walad," as in khashab and khushub. Hassan ibn Thabit has said:

Ya Bakr Amina, blessed is her mention,
from the offspring of a chaste woman, through the luck of the most fortunate.

Most of the people recited "kubbaran" with a shadda on the ba', and it is an intensive form like Hassan. 'Isa said: it is a Yemeni dialect, and upon it is the saying of the poet:

And a man is joined to the youths of generosity
in the manner of the noble, and he is not of the ordinary.

with a damma on the waw. Ibn Muhaysin and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "kubaran" with a light ba', and it is an intensive form, but it is weaker than the first. Ibn Muhaysin, as narrated from him by Abu al-Akhrit Wahb ibn Wadih, recited "kibaran" with a kasra on the kaf. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is the plural of "kabir," as if he made "makr" stand in place of sins, great deeds, and the like.

When they died, the people of that age fashioned their images from stone and said: "We look at them and remember their deeds." That generation perished, and the veneration of the next generation for those stones increased, and so on until they were worshipped. Then those idols, with their very forms, were transferred—and it was said: rather, only the names—to tribes of the Arabs. Nafi' alone recited "wuddan" with a damma on the waw, and this was narrated from 'Asim. The rest, along with al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Talha, Shayba, and Abu Ja'far (with a difference of transmission from the three), recited "wadda" with a fatha on the waw. A poet said:

Wadd greets you, for we are not permitted
the idle pastimes of women, and religion has resolved.

It is said that he meant by this the idol, and it is narrated with both a damma and a fatha on the waw.

Al-A'mash recited "wa-la yaghutha wa-ya'uqa" with tanwin, and this is an error, because the definiteness is inherent and the form is that of a verb.

Al-Jahdari and al-Hasan recited "mimma khatii'atihim" in the singular. Abu 'Amr alone, al-Hasan, 'Isa, al-A'raj, and Qatada (with a difference from them) recited "mimma khataya-hum" in the broken plural. His, the Exalted, saying: "Then they were made to enter a Fire" means Jahannam, and He expressed it with the past tense because the matter is certain. It was also said: he meant their being presented to the Fire morning and evening, and He expressed this as entry. His, the Exalted, saying: "and they found" means that those who were drowned found no one other than Allah, the Exalted, to help them or to turn away from them the might of Allah.

That generation perished, and the veneration of the next generation for those stones increased, and so on until they were worshipped. Then those idols, with their very forms, were transferred—and it was said: rather, only the names—to tribes of the Arabs. Nafi' alone recited "wuddan" with a damma on the waw, and this was narrated from 'Asim. The rest, along with al-A'mash, al-Hasan, Talha, Shayba, and Abu Ja'far (with a difference of transmission from the three), recited "wadda" with a fatha on the waw. A poet said:

Wadd greets you, for we are not permitted

It is said that he meant by this the idol, and it is narrated with both a damma and a fatha on the waw.

Al-A'mash recited "wa-la yaghutha wa-ya'uqa" with tanwin, and this is an error, because the definiteness is inherent and the form is that of a verb.

His saying: "And they have already led many astray" is a report from Nuh (peace be upon him) about them, and it is detached from what he related of their words. The meaning is: these speakers have already led many people astray, including followers and common folk. Then he invoked against them, to God the Exalted, that He not increase them except in error. He mentioned "the wrongdoers" so that the supplication would encompass everyone who follows their path. Al-Jahdari and al-Hasan recited "mimma khatii'atihim" in the singular. Abu 'Amr alone, al-Hasan, 'Isa, al-A'raj, and Qatada (with a difference from them) recited "mimma khataya-hum" in the broken plural. His, the Exalted, saying: "Then they were made to enter a Fire" means Jahannam, and He expressed it with the past tense because the matter is certain. It was also said: he meant their being presented to the Fire morning and evening, and He expressed this as entry. His, the Exalted, saying: "and they found" means that those who were drowned found no one other than Allah, the Exalted, to help them or to turn away from them the might of Allah.

(p-423) The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿And Noah said: "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any dweller from among the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will beget none but wicked, ungrateful disbelievers.﴾ ﴿My Lord, forgive me, my parents, whoever enters my house as a believer, and the believing men and believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction.﴾

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd that Noah, peace be upon him, did not make this supplication until after Allah had brought forth every believer from their loins, and had rendered the wombs of women barren seventy years before the punishment. Qatadah said: and after it had been revealed to him that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed. Previously he had been eager and compassionate toward them. In a hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Some people would strike him at times until he fell unconscious. When he recovered he would say: 'O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

"Dayyar" is originally "diwaran," and it is a fay'al (form) from al-dawaran (revolving, circulating), meaning one who comes and goes. It is said of it: dawwar, whose pattern is fa''al. Dayyar, whose pattern is fayy'al, has the root diwar, as in al-qiwam and al-qiyam.

Most people recite "wa-liwalidayya" (وَلِوالِدَيَّ). Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "wa-li-abawayya" (وَلِأبَوِيَّ). Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "wa-liwalidi" (وَلِوالِدِي) with a kasra on the dal, specifying his father for the supplication. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "No father of Noah was a disbeliever, from the time between him and Adam, peace be upon them both."

Yahya ibn Ya'mur and al-Jahdari recited "wa-liwaladayya" (وَلِوَلَدَيَّ) with a fathah on the lam and a shaddah on the ya with a fathah. This is the recitation of al-Nakha'i. By it he specifies his two sons for the supplication.

"Baytahu" (his house) refers, according to Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of exegetes (mufassirun), to the mosque. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "His house is his law and his religion." He used the metaphor of a house for them, as one says "the dome of Islam" and "the tent-pole of the religion."

It was also said that he meant his ark, and it was said that he meant his dwelling. His saying "and for the believing men and believing women" is a generalization of the supplication to the believers of every nation. Some scholars said: "The one who answered Noah, peace be upon him, so that the disbelieving people of the earth were drowned by his supplication, is worthy of answering him again, so that by his supplication he shows mercy to the believers."

"Tabar" means destruction and the vanishing of traces.

Hafs, from 'Asim, and Hisham and Abu Qurrah, from Nafi', recited "baytiya" (بَيْتِي) with the ya vocalized (with a fathah). The rest recited it with the ya silent (sukun).

The tafsir of Surat [Nuh] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
